title: Dependency Hardening & Canary Criteria Tabletop
summary: Tabletop to align owners and acceptance criteria for dependency hardening and canary rollouts ahead of the private deploy pilot. Discussed canary metric thresholds, rollback triggers, IO/throughput degradation detection, and a trimmed runbook for third-party infra upgrades.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-02
Start: 09:00 PST
Duration: 90 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Aisha Malik, Ethan Liu, Priya Kapoor, Tom Greenwood, Mariana Silva, Kai Jensen, Noah Rivera, Lina Chen

[00:00] Aisha: okay, hey everyone thanks for joining, I know it's a busy week, uh this is a tabletop for dependency hardening and canary criteria — we want to make sure the private pilot has clear gates. I'll run through goals then hand to Ethan for the runbook sketch.
[00:28] Ethan: cool, quick note before we start, I've been seeing some tail latency blips on the staging kv-cache cluster, not catastrophes but enough to worry for a canary. Might affect canary thresholds.
[00:45] Priya: yeah I saw that too, and the p99 is spiky when batching increases, probably due to eviction jitter, so we need to include queue depth metrics not just p95 token latency.
[01:10] Tom: just to ground the convo — objective is to be able to ship the private deploy pilot with a canary that has automated rollback for clear conditions, and human-in-the-loop for ambiguous signals. We need acceptance criteria we can test in staging.
[01:35] Mariana: producers are asking for a short release checklist — minimal gating points so sales/security have something to hold customers to.
[01:50] Kai: and oncall will need a condensed playbook, not a 30-page doc, like 6 steps max to revert and a clear owner.

[02:12] Ethan: okay, proposing three classes of canary metrics: 1) correctness/regression (LLM eval drop / hallucination spike), 2) perf/latency (p50/p95/p99 token latency, queue depth), 3) infra health (GPU memory, nvlink errors, kv-cache eviction rate). We'll attach weights to each.
[02:40] Lina: on correctness, how do we monitor hallucinations automatically? We have the prompt-qa sets but they only catch known regressions. We need runtime detectors — maybe shorter ngram repetition detectors and rate of unknown tokens.
[03:05] Priya: for the pilot, we can use a small prompt corpus with known-good outputs; if eval fail rate > 2% over a 10 minute window that's a hard fail. But for zero-day hallucinations we fall back to anomaly detection.
[03:30] Aisha: 2% sounds reasonable, but let's make it tiered: 2% soft, 5% immediate stop. Document that.

[04:00] Noah: we also need to be careful with batching — we can't tie canary success to a batch size that customers won't use. So include per-request latency baselines.
[04:20] Ethan: agreed, include both per-token and per-request metrics. Also separate synthetic traffic vs real traffic thresholds.

[05:00] Tom: rollback triggers — what are we comfortable automating? For example automatic rollback on p99 latency > 2x baseline for 5 minutes? Or include a second confirmation?
[05:20] Priya: automatic rollback is okay for clear infra failures: gpu OOMs, nvlink errors, disk IO saturation. For performance we should try automatic throttling or traffic reroute before rollback. But if elevated error rate + latency together — auto rollback.
[05:50] Kai: from an oncall POV, we need an automated alert with playbook link and a single-click rollback in the console; if the rollback fails, escalate to Eng Mgr.

[06:30] Lina: runbook sketch: step 0 run health check script (link to doc), step 1 collect p95/p99, step 2 check kv cache eviction logs, step 3 decide rollback if both infra and perf thresholds exceeded, step 4 execute rollback, step 5 validate. We can make the health check run automatically as part of canary pipeline.
[07:05] Mariana: add a stakeholder notification template for legal and sales, inc incident severity and customer impact.

[07:40] Ethan: I'm going to propose concrete thresholds as a starting point: correctness soft fail 2% eval mismatch (10 min sliding), hard fail 5% (3 min), p99 > 2x baseline for 5 minutes is soft, 4x for 3 minutes is hard. KV eviction > 0.5% sustained over 5 minutes. Those numbers are draft.
[08:15] Tom: we should annotate thresholds with rationale and test plan. E.g., 2% was based on historical minor drift seen in last quant cycles.

[09:00] Aisha: what about third-party dependency upgrades — e.g., new cuDNN, driver, or model-client libraries? That was part of the "dependency hardening" scope.
[09:20] Ethan: yeah, upgrade windows must be tested in an isolated canary pool; we must run a regression matrix: short latency runs, longer throughput runs and KV stress. Also we need pinned kernel fallback tests because we saw earlier that some kernels regress.
[09:45] Priya: and include a compatibility test against older pinned weights to ensure that quantized paths still produce acceptable outputs. Sometimes quantization kernels diverge.

[10:15] Lina: I ran a small matrix last week — one driver bump increased tokenization variance for a small subset, it didn't break correctness but increased generation time by ~8% p95. That would have tripped our perf thresholds.
[10:35] Noah: that suggests we need a dependency change gating policy: if any infra dependency changes, run full canary pipeline including correctness eval before promoting.

[11:00] Mariana: we should capture stakeholder sign-offs for infra vs model upgrades differently. Model changes require product sign-off; infra changes require infra + QE + SRE.
[11:20] Tom: agree, add an approvals field in the release gating doc. We'll also include a rollback owner for each change type.

[12:05] Ethan: a practical question — how long should a canary run be to be meaningful? We can't run canaries for 24 hrs for every push. For perf we can do 30-60 minutes with synthetic traffic plus 2 hours of sampled real traffic for correctness sampling. Thoughts?
[12:30] Priya: for initial pilot, 60 min synthetic + 2 hours sampled live is a good balance. We'll define the sample rate to keep customer impact low.

[13:05] Aisha: okay, put that in the runbook. Now on observability gaps — Lina you flagged missing query tagging for model variant and kernel path?
[13:25] Lina: yes, we often lose kernel path in traces; need a low-overhead tag in the runtime so dashboards can break down by kernel. Also need a quick dashboard for canary that overlays p99/p95, error rate, kv eviction, and a small correctness eval panel.
[13:50] Ethan: I'm thinking a canary dashboard composed template that we can instantiate per canary job. We'll put it in Grafana and have an ephemeral link in the canary job.

[14:15] Kai: for oncall, add a single condensed dashboard with a red/amber/green status computed from weighted metrics so they don't have to interpret 10 panels during an incident.
[14:35] Priya: automation can compute weighted status but we must show the raw signals too. Also include an 'explain' button that gives recent examples of failed eval prompts.

[15:05] Tom: let's talk about communication — what does sales/security want when a canary fails? Mariana?
[15:20] Mariana: brief template: incident severity, brief technical cause (if known), customers impacted, mitigation (rollback done/traffic routed), ETA for resolution. Keep it two bullets for execs and attach runbook log. We'll maintain a centralized incident folder.
[15:45] Aisha: good. Also, legal asked for audit logs of who triggered rollbacks and the canary job run outputs — we must capture those automatically.

[16:10] Ethan: we can attach the canary job artifact (metrics snapshot, traces, sample outputs) to the rollback action in the console. That should satisfy audit.

[16:40] Lina: quick note on tests — I'll run a KV cache chaos suite that simulates eviction storms and measure p95/p99 across sequences. If we see consistent degradation > 20% p99, that's a red flag.

[17:10] Priya: and we'll simulate partial GPU loss via node drainage to test autoscaling/fallback. Confirm that model fallback variant doesn't produce a correctness drop > 5%.

[17:35] Aisha: okay, let's capture the tentative acceptance criteria on the board: correctness soft/hard, latency soft/hard, infra signals, third-party gating, canary duration, observability template, audit logs, and stakeholder sign-offs.

[18:05] Tom: before we wrap, two open risk items: 1) KV cache eviction detection coverage — is our instrumentation sufficient? 2) Runbook complexity — need to keep oncall steps minimal.
[18:25] Priya: for 1) Lina will instrument and report; for 2) Aisha and Mariana will refine the playbook to 6 steps max and produce a one-pager for oncall.

[18:50] Aisha: great. Any final comments?
[19:05] Kai: just emphasize we need a one-click rollback button in the console with confirmation and audit. It's critical.
[19:20] Ethan: noted. I'll include a UI story for the console team.

[19:40] Aisha: thanks everyone. Quick recap of next steps and owners in the doc and I'll follow up with calendar invites for the cross-team tabletop on 2026-12-15.

[20:00] (meeting ends)

Notes about transcript quality: occasional speaker mislabels and slight ASR errors in technical terms (nvlink sometimes transcribed as n-link, kv-cache as key-v cache). References: canary runbook draft (link: https://redwood.internal/docs/canary-runbook-draft), release gating checklist (link: https://redwood.internal/docs/release-gate), kv chaos job (link: https://redwood.internal/jobs/kv-chaos).
